[2, 4] The outbreak primarily impacted young, healthy Hispanic/Latino women, with reports suggesting that insurance barriers may have been a factor in their seeking medical tourism. [1] The situation resulted in a high mortality rate; one report cited a 40% mortality rate among identified cases, while another noted 8 deaths among 31 suspected, probable, and confirmed U.S. cases. [1, 3] The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), in collaboration with the Mexican Ministry of Health and state and local health departments, continued to investigate and provide updates on the matter. [4] <2> A report published in the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) on September 29, 2023, detailed the findings of a survey of U.S. healthcare providers on their vaccination recommendations for women of reproductive age. [1, 2] The survey, known as the Fall 2022 DocStyles survey, was conducted to understand the prevalence of COVID-19 vaccination attitudes and practices among healthcare providers caring for this demographic. [2, 3] The analysis showed that while a high percentage of providers recommended COVID-19, influenza, and Tdap vaccines, there were variations in practices across different medical specialties. [1, 2] Overall, 82.9% of providers reported recommending COVID-19 vaccination to women of reproductive age, but only 54.7% offered or administered the vaccine in their practice. [2, 3] Among providers who care for pregnant patients, most recommended all three vaccines (COVID-19: 82.9%; influenza: 89.4%; and Tdap: 78.1%). [2, 6] Specifically for COVID-19 vaccination in pregnant patients, Obstetrician-Gynecologists (94.2%) were more likely to recommend it than family practitioners or internists (82.1%). [1, 3] The findings are intended to inform and guide outreach strategies to improve vaccine confidence and increase vaccination coverage among women of reproductive age, particularly pregnant individuals. [1, 3] <3> In the summer of 2023, the United States witnessed a resurgence of COVID-19, marked by increasing hospitalizations and cases. This wave was driven by circulating Omicron subvariants, with EG.5 (nicknamed 'Eris') emerging as the dominant strain, accounting for 21.5% of new infections by September 1, 2023. Following EG.5 was the FL.1.5.1 variant, making up 14.5% of cases. Concurrently, health officials and the World Health Organization began monitoring a new, highly mutated variant, BA.2.86 (nicknamed 'Pirola'), which was first detected in the U.S. in Michigan on August 3, 2023. While the summer surge was attributed to XBB lineage viruses like EG.5, the potential impact of BA.2.86 was initially uncertain due to its significant number of mutations. However, the CDC stated in early September that the increases in hospitalizations were not being driven by BA.2.86. <4> On September 12, 2023, the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) voted 13-1 to recommend the updated 2023–2024 monovalent XBB.1.5-derived COVID-19 vaccine for universal use in all individuals aged 6 months and older. The recommendation, subsequently endorsed by the CDC, is intended to provide protection against severe illness and death from the COVID-19 variants circulating at the time. Evidence presented indicated that over 90% of circulating viruses belonged to the XBB lineage, and data from vaccine manufacturers showed the updated vaccine induces a broad immune response against variants including XBB.1.5, XBB.1.16, EG.5.1, and BA.2.86. <5> In the lead-up to the 2023-2024 influenza season, public health organizations and vaccine manufacturers issued forecasts and recommendations. A key piece of guidance was for the public to get vaccinated by the end of October 2023. For the season, all available flu vaccines in the US were quadrivalent, designed to protect against two influenza A viruses and two influenza B viruses. <6> On September 5, 2023, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a Health Alert Network (HAN) advisory to notify clinicians of increased Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) activity in the Southeastern United States. [1, 2, 4, 9] The advisory noted rising case numbers and hospitalizations, particularly in Florida and Georgia, suggesting a return to pre-COVID-19 pandemic seasonal trends. [1, 4, 7] Historically, such regional increases have signaled the beginning of the national RSV season, with the virus typically spreading north and west over the subsequent two to three months. [1, 6, 7] The CDC urged clinicians to prepare for the 2023-2024 RSV season by implementing new prevention options, including monoclonal antibody products like nirsevimab for infants and young children, and two new vaccines (RSVPreF3 and RSVpreF) for adults aged 60 and older. [1, 4, 8] <7> On September 1, 2023, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a Health Alert Network (HAN) Health Advisory to notify healthcare providers, laboratories, and the public about severe and fatal *Vibrio vulnificus* infections. [4, 7] The alert was prompted by an increase in cases during July and August 2023, a period marked by widespread heat waves and above-average coastal sea surface temperatures. [4, 9] During this two-month span, 11 severe infections were reported across three East Coast states: seven in North Carolina, two in Connecticut, and two in New York. [2, 3, 6] These infections, which resulted in five deaths, were primarily associated with the exposure of open wounds to coastal waters or, in some instances, handling or consuming raw seafood. [3, 5, 8] The CDC urged healthcare professionals to consider *V. vulnificus* in cases of infected wounds exposed to coastal waters, especially as warming temperatures may lead to a rise in such infections. [1, 3] A total of 18 people across four states—New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, and Maryland—were infected, with seven requiring hospitalization. Subsequently, on April 1, 2024, the Texas Department of State Health Services and the CDC reported a human case of H5N1 in a dairy farm worker. This marked the second-ever human case of H5N1 recorded in the United States, but it was the first believed to be transmitted from a mammal (cattle) to a human. The patient, who had direct contact with dairy cows presumed to be infected, experienced conjunctivitis (eye inflammation) as their only symptom and was treated with an antiviral medication. Health officials have stated that the risk to the general public remains low. <2> The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a Health Alert Network (HAN) advisory on March 28, 2024, to notify healthcare providers of an increase in invasive meningococcal disease. As of March 25, 2024, 143 cases had been reported for the year, a significant rise from the 81 cases reported by the same time in 2023. The total of 422 cases in 2023 was the highest annual number since 2014. The increase is primarily attributed to *Neisseria meningitidis* serogroup Y, specifically the ST-1466 strain. This strain is disproportionately affecting people aged 30–60, Black or African American individuals, and people with HIV. The presentations will cover Pfizer's infectious disease portfolio, featuring research on COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), pneumococcal disease, and Lyme disease. The company's announcement of its participation and the details of its presentations was made on October 13, 2025. <4> Pfizer and BioNTech announced on August 27, 2025, that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved their supplemental Biologics License Application (sBLA) for the LP.8.1-adapted monovalent COVID-19 vaccine, known as COMIRNATY®. This updated 2025-2026 vaccine formula targets the SARS-CoV-2 sublineage LP.8.1, in line with FDA guidance to more closely match circulating strains. The approval applies to adults aged 65 and older, and individuals from 5 through 64 years old who have at least one underlying condition that puts them at high risk for severe COVID-19 outcomes. The companies confirmed that shipments of the new vaccine would begin immediately to ensure availability in pharmacies, hospitals, and clinics across the U.S. in the following days. The FDA's decision was based on a comprehensive body of evidence demonstrating the vaccine platform's safety and efficacy, including preclinical data that showed the LP.8.1-adapted vaccine generated improved immune responses against multiple circulating sublineages compared to previous versions. <5> The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) released its initial outlook for the 2025-2026 respiratory disease season, which is defined as October through mid-May. The report predicts a combined peak hospitalization rate for COVID-19, influenza, and RSV that is similar to the 2024-2025 season. However, the CDC anticipates that the peak weekly hospitalization rate for COVID-19 could be similar to or higher than the previous season. This is particularly true if a new variant with moderate immune escape emerges. For influenza, a season of moderate severity is expected. The outlook is based on a combination of historical data, expert opinion, and scenario modeling. The CDC plans to update this outlook every two months throughout the season as new data becomes available. <6> A new CDC analysis of national surveillance data from October 2020 through September 2024 has identified consistent seasonal peaks in COVID-19 activity in the United States. The report confirms biannual surges, with peaks occurring in the late summer months of July through September and again in the winter from December to February. Researchers noted that this seasonality highlights the importance of vaccination schedules for those at elevated risk for severe infection, as vaccine-induced antibodies typically wane within three to six months. The findings are intended to help improve forecasting and preparedness for future waves of the virus. <7> In a report published on August 8, 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed an additional pediatric death from influenza. [7] The death occurred during the week ending April 19, 2025. [2, 7] This event brought the total number of pediatric flu deaths for the 2024-2025 season to 267, the highest recorded total for any non-pandemic year since pediatric flu deaths became a reportable condition in 2004. [7] Of the children whose vaccination status was known, 90% who died from influenza were not fully vaccinated. [7] <8> World Rabies Day is observed globally to raise awareness about rabies prevention and control.; Events often include educational campaigns to work toward the goal of zero human rabies deaths.; Events often include pet vaccination clinics to work toward the goal of zero human rabies deaths. <9> A CDC report published on July 31, 2025, revealed a continued nationwide decline in vaccination rates among kindergartners for the 2024-2025 school year. [1, 2, 3] This decrease was observed across all reported vaccines, marking a continuation of a multi-year trend. [4, 5] Specifically, the coverage for the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine fell to 92.5%, moving the rate further away from the 95% national target required to prevent community transmission and maintain herd immunity. [6, 7] <10> Researchers at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) have shown for the first time that a common type of human papillomavirus (HPV) found on the skin, known as beta-HPV, can directly cause cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), a form of skin cancer. This discovery, published in The New England Journal of Medicine, challenges the previous belief that beta-HPV only facilitated skin damage caused by ultraviolet (UV) radiation. The finding stems from the case of a 34-year-old woman with a rare genetic condition that weakened her T-cell function, leading to recurrent and aggressive cSCC. Genetic analysis of her tumors revealed that beta-HPV had integrated into the cancer cells' DNA and was driving their growth, a mechanism previously unobserved for this type of HPV. Following a stem cell transplant that restored her T-cell function, the patient's cancer and other HPV-related conditions resolved, confirming that her compromised immune system allowed the virus to cause the cancer. This breakthrough could significantly change the understanding and treatment of cSCC, particularly for immunocompromised individuals, suggesting that immune-targeting therapies may be beneficial.
